title: Can you know?
hook: some traditions stress confident assurance of salvation; others a humble hope

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace and cooperation: a sail and the wind, and Mary's yes. Your line was grace and yes. What small step did you take? Day one thousand ninety-one.

Midnight, in a prison in the town of Philippi. Two prisoners, Paul and Silas, are singing hymns in the dark with their feet in the stocks. Then the ground heaves. An earthquake throws the doors open and shakes the chains loose. The jailer wakes, sees the open doors, and draws his sword to kill himself, sure his prisoners are gone. Paul shouts: we are all here. The jailer runs in with a light, falls down trembling, and asks: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" Paul's answer is short. But some readers hear a second question under the jailer's: once I've answered, can I know? Today's word: assurance.
screen: `WHAT MUST I DO TO BE SAVED?`

segments.voice: Assurance means a settled confidence. Here, a confidence that you belong to God and are safe with him. Paul answers the jailer: "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house." John's first letter even says why it was written: "that ye may know that ye have eternal life." May know. Not guess. And Paul, in Romans, runs through a list: death, life, angels, things present, things to come. He says none of it "shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Reformed, Methodist and evangelical churches stress this: you can rest in what God has promised, and know it. But the same Paul writes in another letter that he disciplines himself, "lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway." And to the Romans: "For we are saved by hope." Catholic teaching says a person can have firm hope and real confidence in God's mercy, but without claiming certainty about one's own final state, unless God reveals it. Orthodox teachers describe salvation as a road still being walked, and speak with a humble hope rather than a settled claim. So some churches stress confidence, and some stress humility, and both point to the same God. Here is where they meet. John again: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear." Whether a church says I know or I hope, neither one is meant to run on fear. And the jailer? That same night, Acts says, he washed their wounds, and set food before them, and rejoiced.

Here's the practice: rest in trust, not worry. Settle, and breathe. Notice where worry sits in your body right now: the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach. Let it be there. Then let one line from today come back: nothing shall be able to separate us. Or simply: no fear in love. Breathe it in. Let the shoulders drop a little on the out-breath. If you pray, you can rest in God's promise. If you don't, just practice resting, without having to solve anything first. The bell holds the time.
Assurance. A settled confidence of belonging to God. Some churches stress a sure knowing, others a humble hope, and both refuse to be ruled by fear.
Your line: trust, not fear. When worry starts its loop today, interrupt it once with one line: no fear in love. Day one thousand ninety-one.

howItsDone: Evangelical and Reformed churches teach believers that they can be assured of salvation through God's promises, while Catholic and Orthodox Christians speak of a confident, humble hope, nourished by prayer and the sacraments.

Catholic position summarized from Trent Session 6 chs. 9 and 12 (no certainty of faith about being in grace or of final perseverance without special revelation) and the virtue of hope. Confirm fairness.
Orthodox description ('a road still being walked', 'humble hope') is general; an Orthodox Keeper should confirm or reword.
'Reformed, Methodist and other evangelical Christians stress this strongly': general claims; consider softening. Wesley's own assurance experience is kept for tomorrow's day (sanctification).
Acts 16:33–34: washed their stripes, set meat before them, rejoiced. Paraphrased. Note the text says 'set meat', rendered 'food'.
Original πληροφορία: Hebrews 10:22 KJV 'full assurance of faith'; confirm accent and pronunciation.

Editor pass: 'a Roman prison' trimmed to 'a prison' (Acts 16 does not call it Roman); cut the stock 'the one that keeps people up at night' for 'some readers hear a second question'; 'lists everything he can think of' rephrased as 'runs through a list'; the jailer's meal now credited to Acts rather than to Luke by name (authorship is tradition, not stated in the text).
